grammar.title: Gramatyka
grammar.rule: To jest klucz. Jan ma klucz. To jest rysunek, nie zamek.
grammar.note_en:
Polish has no articles corresponding to English “a” or “the”. Klucz can mean “a key” or “the key”; the situation tells you which. To jest klucz means “This is a key”. Here to points to something being identified, while jest means “is”. In To jest rysunek, nie zamek (“This is a drawing, not a lock”), nie rejects the proposed identity. That is different from saying that a thing is missing; the chapter does not yet teach that construction. To itself stays the same with the nouns in these naming sentences: To jest pudełko means “This is a box”. The table is a reference, not a form-filling task.

A noun names a person or thing. The nominative is the noun form used for naming and for the subject, the person or thing the sentence is about. An adjective describes a noun: mały klucz means “a small key”; duży zamek means “a large lock”. Mały and duży here describe one masculine noun. Grammatical gender is a property of the noun, not of the object's sex. Do not attach these exact endings to every noun: pudełko is neuter, and its adjective forms come later.

A verb expresses an action or state. Jan ma klucz means “Jan has a key”. Ala rysuje klucz means “Ala draws a key”. The thing affected by an action is called its direct object; Polish normally uses the accusative case for that job. In this chapter, the masculine inanimate objects klucz, zamek, rysunek, papier, ołówek and znak have the same spelling as when they are named. Thus the key does not change in To jest klucz (“This is a key”) and Jan ma klucz (“Jan has a key”). This is a bounded set of examples, not a claim that Polish objects never change their ending. Person names and neuter objects are not practised in this construction yet. Negated objects and complemented searching also wait for later teaching.

Czeka means “waits/is waiting”; szuka means “searches/is searching”; patrzy means “looks/is looking”. Rysuje means “draws/is drawing”; przesuwa “moves/slides”; obraca “turns”; pokazuje “shows/points out”. These are third-person singular forms: they describe Ala or Jan, one person, rather than “I”, “you” or a group. English often uses “is drawing” where Polish uses this single present-tense form. Once the subject is clear, Polish can leave the name out, as in Pokazuje mały znak (“[He] shows the small mark”). This is not a command.

Tu means “here”, tam “there”, and teraz “now”. The location sequence keeps Jan as the observer while the paper moves away and the key remains near him. The words refer to that observer, not fixed sides of every page. Gdzie jest zamek? means “Where is the lock?” Co to jest? means “What is this?” Czy begins a question that can be answered tak (“yes”) or nie (“no”): Czy to jest mały klucz? means “Is this a small key?” I links things or actions (“and”); ale contrasts them (“but”). In the story, the paper is not the box itself: rysunek means the drawing, papier the paper carrying it. The small circle is a znak, a mark; comparing that mark changes where Ala and Jan look next.

Keep Polish spelling when you write: ł in ołówek and stół is a distinct letter, not l. The normaliser gives a spelling hint rather than treating missing diacritics as the canonical spelling. Ordinary Polish word stress is on the second-to-last syllable; there are exceptions, taught when met. Audio is suspended. The pencil is ołówek, a drawing rysunek, a sheet/material of paper papier, and a table stół. The vocabulary cards show only the present forms actually read here, with citation infinitives as dictionary labels rather than extra story grammar.

The naming table means, row by row: “This is a key”; “This is a drawing”; “This is a box”; “This is paper”. The size table contrasts mały klucz (“a small key”) with duży klucz (“a large key”), and mały zamek (“a small lock”) with duży zamek (“a large lock”). The action table reads: Ala czeka (“Ala waits”), Jan szuka (“Jan searches”), Jan ma klucz (“Jan has a key”), Jan pokazuje klucz (“Jan shows the key”), Jan obraca papier (“Jan turns the sheet”), Ala rysuje klucz (“Ala draws a key”).

items.rubric: Name an object Jan holds in the opening section: key, paper or pencil. Keep Jan as the person asked about; other true objects and word orders are valid.
Ala draws a key and copies its mark in the opening section. Naming either or both is valid; do not attribute Jan’s small-lock sketch to her.
Identify the paper Jan turns to show its two sides. A different word order is fine; a claim that he turns the physical box is not shown.
At this stage Jan points out the drawing and its mark, not a discovered physical box. Either relevant drawing detail is valid.
Ala slides the concealing paper away, revealing the real box. She later moves the key too; either action is valid if its moment is clear.
The final physical box lock bears the circular mark matching the key. Name that mark; a truthful short Polish sentence and other word orders are valid.
